Session plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Teachers leave knowing why the relationship carries the learning in high school, with a short list of ways to connect that have nothing to do with the schoolwork, a plan for the student who has checked out of the work, a way to repair things after a rough moment, and two or three names to start with.

Materials

  • Index cards, one per teacher
  • Each teacher's class rosters (on a laptop or printed)
  • The faculty quick reference (last slide), printed or linked

Flow

  1. 5 minOpening: your favorite high school teacher
  2. 8 minThe research: why the relationship carries the learning
  3. 4 minWhat teenagers need from adults
  4. 8 minConnection outside the schoolwork
  5. 5 minThe student who has checked out of the work
  6. 4 minWhen it goes sideways: repair
  7. 7 minWho do you know? (roster exercise)
  8. 4 minTwo or three names

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Thirty minutes: the opening card (3), the research, two slides only (5), what teenagers need (3), connection outside the schoolwork (7), checked out of the work (4), who do you know (5), two or three names (3). Skip repair or give it one sentence. Share the faculty quick reference afterward.

Before you present
Nobody here is cold.

Most teachers already connect with plenty of students. Say so early. This talk is about the students we haven't reached yet, and about doing more of what already works, on purpose.

Connection isn't friendship.

Warm and professional go together. Keep conversations in public spaces or with the door open, keep messages on school channels, and stay the adult in the room. Students want a teacher who's on their side, not a buddy.

You can't be close to 120 students.

Nobody can. The aim is that every student has something with you: you know their name, one thing about them, and they know you noticed. A few will need more, and that's where the roster exercise helps.

Two minutes, not a program.

If Kids Do Well If They Can ran earlier, connect the dots: the two-minute habit from that talk is one of these moves. Don't re-teach it; point back to it.

When a student tells you something heavy.

Closeness means students tell you things. If a student shares something about safety, harm or home that worries you, walk them to the counseling office that day. You don't have to carry it, and you shouldn't promise to keep it secret.

Teachers have limits too.

Connection takes energy. A teacher who is running on empty will connect less, and that's a signal to take care of the teacher, not a failing. Name that warmly.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

We connect fastest with students like us.

Gehlbach's study shows similarity builds closeness, which means the students who share our background, interests or style get more of us by default. Look at the roster for who's missing, and go find something you share with them.

Names.

Ask each student how to say their name, practice it, and use it. Don't shorten or anglicize it unless the student asks you to. A name said right is the cheapest, clearest sign that a student belongs.

What respect looks like varies.

In some families, children are taught to keep a respectful distance from teachers, avoid eye contact with adults, or never talk about home. A quiet student may be showing respect, not disinterest. Let them set the pace.

Show up across the whole school.

Games are easy to find. So are plays. Robotics, a debate round, a cultural club's event, a student's art in the hallway count too. If a student invites you to something from their community, it's an honor; go if you can.

Not every student can stay after.

Students who work, ride a late bus, care for siblings or live far away can't hang around after class. Build connection into the minutes you already have with them.

Don't assume.

Ask open questions ("Anything fun this weekend?"), not ones that assume a family, holiday, religion, money or dating life. LGBTQ+ students, students in foster care, and students with a parent who's gone notice these questions.

Side by side works for some.

Some students, including many neurodivergent students, find face-to-face talk hard. Walking together, working on something with your hands, or a quick written note can work better than eye contact and questions.

What the research says

Across 99 studies from preschool through high school, warm teacher-student relationships were linked to student engagement (medium to large) and achievement (small to medium), and conflict-filled ones to lower engagement and achievement. Overall, the links were stronger in the higher grades.

Roorda, Koomen, Spilt and Oort, Review of Educational Research, 2011

An update pooling 189 studies and about 249,000 students found engagement is part of the bridge between the relationship and achievement. The link between warm relationships and engagement was stronger in secondary school than in primary school.

Roorda, Jak, Zee, Oort and Koomen, School Psychology Review, 2017

A meta-analysis of 119 studies and 355,325 students found learner-centered teacher qualities (warmth, empathy, encouraging thinking) correlated with student outcomes at r = .31, above average for educational practices, especially for engagement and behavior.

Cornelius-White, Review of Educational Research, 2007

In a randomized trial of My Teaching Partner-Secondary, teachers got about twice-monthly coaching on their interactions with students (not their content). In the year after coaching, their students' achievement rose by the equivalent of moving from the 50th to the 59th percentile. About a third of teachers dropped out after randomization, so the What Works Clearinghouse rates it as meeting standards with reservations.

Allen, Pianta, Gregory, Mikami and Lun, Science, 2011

In 86 secondary classrooms, teachers coached through My Teaching Partner had no significant gap in discipline referrals between Black students and their classmates, while control classrooms kept the gap.

Gregory, Hafen, Ruzek, Mikami, Allen and Pianta, School Psychology Review, 2016

315 ninth graders and their 25 teachers filled out a get-to-know-you survey. When teachers learned five things they shared with specific students, they rated those relationships better, and those students earned higher course grades. The effects were largest for underserved students (one school; the authors call this part exploratory).

Gehlbach et al., Journal of Educational Psychology, 2016

Following 2,079 high school students for a year, each additional positive relationship with a teacher went with more engagement, and the benefit of positive relationships outweighed the harm of negative ones.

Martin and Collie, Journal of Educational Psychology, 2019

In a national sample of about 14,800 people, feeling connected to school as a teenager was linked to less emotional distress, suicidal thinking, violence and drug misuse in adulthood. Teens high in both school and family connectedness had 48 to 66 percent lower odds of these outcomes.

Steiner et al., Pediatrics, 2019 (Add Health data; associations, not proof of cause)

Prevention programs that lecture often fail with teenagers because they clash with a stronger adolescent need for respect and status. Approaches that treat teens with respect and give them real standing do better.

Yeager, Dahl and Dweck, Perspectives on Psychological Science, 2018

Discipline-referred high school students were more cooperative and less defiant with teachers who took a relational approach, and trust explained the link. A small, correlational study (32 teachers, 32 students).

Gregory and Ripski, School Psychology Review, 2008

Establish-Maintain-Restore (build the relationship, keep it up, repair it after conflict) improved teacher-reported relationships, time on task and disruptive behavior in 4th and 5th grade classrooms. A high school pilot of an adapted version found no significant effects on motivation or engagement, so treat the repair step as sensible practice for teens rather than proven.

Cook et al., School Psychology Review, 2018; Equity-Explicit EMR pilot, 2022

Warm demanders pair warmth with a firm expectation of effort and respect. The caring relationship is what lets them hold a high bar.

Bondy and Ross, Educational Leadership, 2008

Interviews with 96 students in grades 3 to 10 found every group tied its best teacher relationships to teachers who were kind, caring, helpful or funny. Students with a history of disruptive behavior mostly remembered negative relationships, and up to a third couldn't recall a single positive one.

Van Bergen, Sweller and Graham, School Psychology Review, 2020

Relationship mapping (staff list every student, mark the ones no adult knows well, and volunteer to reach out) is a free practice from Harvard's Making Caring Common. It's widely used; it hasn't been tested in a controlled trial.

Making Caring Common, Harvard Graduate School of Education
